title: What Happens to Your Body When You Exercise?
paragraphs: Within seconds of starting to exercise, your body begins to adjust. Your heart rate and breathing increase, pushing more oxygen-rich blood towards the working muscles, while blood vessels in those muscles widen and blood flow to less active organs, such as the digestive system, is temporarily reduced.

Muscles convert oxygen and stored fuel, mainly glucose and fat, into usable energy. Much of that energy is released as heat, so your core temperature rises and your sweat glands become active. If the effort is very intense, muscles also rely partly on processes that do not need oxygen, which is one reason they start to burn and tire.

The brain benefits too. Physical activity increases blood flow to the brain and triggers the release of chemicals, including endorphins, that are associated with improved mood and lower stress. Research consistently links regular exercise with better sleep, sharper attention and a lower risk of depression.

With regular training, the heart pumps more blood with each beat, so your resting heart rate tends to fall, and muscles and bones grow stronger. The World Health Organization advises adults to do at least 150 to 300 minutes of moderate activity a week, plus muscle-strengthening exercise on two or more days.
